opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to understand is that you can't really plan breakthroughs. You can create the conditions for them, but you can't schedule them. So the way a research lab is organized matters enormously.

What I've always advocated is a fairly clear separation between fundamental research and product development, but with a good interface between the two. If you put researchers directly under product pressure, with quarterly deliverables, they will only work on incremental things, because that's what's predictable. The really important ideas often take five, ten years to mature. Convolutional nets, for example: the basic ideas were there in the late eighties, and it took a couple of decades before the hardware, the data, and the community were ready for them to really take off.

So the research side needs freedom. It needs to be able to work on long-term problems, and it needs to be open. I'm a big believer in open research: publish your papers, release your code, open-source your models. People sometimes think that's giving away your advantage, but it's the opposite. You attract the best people, because good scientists want their work to be seen and used. You get feedback from the whole community. And progress goes faster when everyone builds on each other's work. Nobody has a monopoly on good ideas.

Then you need a mechanism to transfer things into products. That usually means an intermediate group, people who understand the research well enough to take a promising prototype and make it robust, scalable, and useful. That part is engineering, and it's hard; it's not something you can just throw over the wall. Sometimes the best way to transfer a technology is to transfer people. A researcher who developed something moves over to the product side for a while and carries the know-how with them.

Finally, you need patience from leadership. The return on fundamental research is enormous, but it's lumpy and unpredictable. Many companies have had great research labs that invented amazing things, and then someone else commercialized them, because the connection to product wasn't there. Other labs got so tied to product that they stopped doing anything truly new. The trick is to hold both: real freedom to explore, and real pathways to impact.

r001.rationale: The response advocates open research, including publishing papers and releasing code and models, and says this helps attract talent and speed progress.

r002.rationale: It separates fundamental research from product development and describes an intermediate group taking a promising prototype and making it robust, scalable, and useful.

r003.rationale: It calls the engineering handoff hard and says labs can invent important things that others commercialize when the connection to products is missing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you can't plan breakthroughs. You can only create the conditions where they become more likely. So the way I've always thought about running a research lab, at FAIR and before that at Bell Labs, is that you hire the best people you can find, you give them a lot of freedom, and you let them work on long-term problems without demanding a product roadmap every quarter. The moment you ask researchers to justify every project in terms of next year's revenue, you've killed the breakthrough before it exists.

But freedom alone isn't enough. The second ingredient is openness. Research that stays locked inside a company doesn't get better. It needs to be published, criticized, reproduced, built upon by people outside your walls. When we open-sourced PyTorch, or released the LLaMA models, a lot of people inside the company asked why we would give that away. The answer is that the ecosystem that grows around open tools comes back to you many times over. Your own researchers become more productive, you attract better people, and the field as a whole moves faster, which is ultimately where the value comes from.

Then there's the question of how an idea actually crosses over into a product. My experience is that this almost never happens by a research lab finishing something and tossing it over the wall. It happens when there's a continuum. You need people who sit in between, applied researchers and engineers who understand the science well enough to see which ideas are ready and which are five years away. At Meta, FAIR sits on one side, product groups on the other, and the applied groups in between are where convolutional nets became the thing that filters content, or where a translation paper became the system people actually use.

And one thing I insist on is to tolerate failure. Most research projects don't pan out. If you punish that, people start working only on safe, incremental things, and you lose precisely the ambitious bets that occasionally change everything. The convolutional net sat around for almost twenty years before the hardware and the data caught up. If someone had been measuring my impact on a two-year horizon in the nineties, they would have concluded it was a dead end.

So the short version is this. Hire great people, protect their time, make them publish, build bridges to the product side rather than walls, and be patient. The practical innovations come out of that almost as a side effect. They're very hard to get if you aim at them directly.

r001.rationale: The response calls openness a key ingredient and explains that publishing, criticism, and outside contributions help the field and innovation advance.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes research from product development by describing applied researchers and engineers who identify which research ideas are ready and help turn them into usable systems.

r003.rationale: It says research projects often fail and rejects handing research over to product groups, but does not identify the transition to substantial engineering as a point where projects often fail.

astra-6.text:
Well, you need both freedom and a path to implementation. Research is inherently uncertain. If you require every project to justify itself with a product roadmap, you’re going to get incremental improvements, but you may miss the ideas that open up entirely new possibilities.

So give researchers room to pursue long-term questions, and then create opportunities for them to work closely with engineers and people who understand real problems. A promising result in a controlled experiment is only the beginning. Can you make it reliable? Can you make it efficient? Does it actually solve a useful problem?

And this should be a feedback loop. Trying to build something often reveals a scientific question you hadn’t anticipated. You want ideas, people, and problems to move in both directions. The lab’s job is to make that interaction easy without making immediate commercial success the criterion for every research decision.

r001.rationale: The response calls for research freedom and easy interaction, but does not state that a culture of openness is necessary for breakthrough innovation.

r002.rationale: It describes a promising controlled experiment as only the beginning, then distinguishes the work of making the result reliable, efficient, and useful.

r003.rationale: The response discusses working with engineers, but does not identify the transition to substantial engineering as a point where innovation projects often fail.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think you have to distinguish research from product development, while making sure there is a connection between the two. Research is inherently uncertain. If you ask researchers to promise a useful product on a particular schedule, they will work on things that are predictable, and you may miss the important breakthroughs.

So you give researchers freedom to pursue ambitious ideas, but you also create opportunities for those ideas to meet real problems. That means researchers and engineers working together, building prototypes, discovering what works at scale and what is still missing. A demonstration is not a product. There is often a tremendous amount of engineering between the two.

And the process is not entirely linear. Sometimes a practical obstacle raises a new scientific question. You want that feedback to flow in both directions. The lab should protect long-term exploration and make it easy for people to collaborate when an idea becomes promising enough to use.

r001.rationale: It advocates researcher freedom and collaboration, but does not clearly state that a culture of openness is necessary for breakthrough innovation.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes a research demonstration from a product and says substantial engineering is needed to turn one into the other.

r003.rationale: It notes that considerable engineering lies between a demonstration and a product, but does not say projects often fail at that transition.
